title: Git Basics: Your First Repository

checkpoint_1.notes: Correct Git version identification (2.51.2—very current). Excellent insight on macOS developer demographics and Unix foundation. Accurate understanding of Homebrew's advantages for package management and version control.

checkpoint_2.notes: Exemplary Git configuration (LFS, VS Code editor, global .gitignore). Perfect understanding of identity requirements (authorship, accountability, contributions graph). Clear explanation of global vs. local config scopes.

checkpoint_3.notes: Proper .git directory verification. Complete understanding of consequences of deletion. Accurate explanation of hidden directory convention (accidental deletion prevention, visual clarity, Unix tradition).

checkpoint_4.notes: Demonstrated problem-solving flexibility (echo vs touch). Perfect git status interpretation showing staged vs untracked files. Outstanding explanation of staging area purpose—grasped the concept of selective commits enabling logical history. Ahead of many junior developers.

checkpoint_5.notes: Correct commit history output. Accurate explanation of commit ID purpose (uniqueness, content-based, tamper-proof, referencing). Professional-grade commit message following Conventional Commits format.

checkpoint_6.notes: 4 commits with professional messages (exceeded requirements). Bonus challenge completed (.gitignore). Excellent attention to detail (notes.txt continuity observation). Balanced reflection showing command familiarity + new tool exposure (git log, echo).

key_takeaways: Git installation and configuration establishes professional development environment
The three-state model (working directory → staging area → repository) is Git's core workflow
The staging area enables selective commits for clean, logical history
Commit messages are documentation—use Conventional Commits format
git status and git log are essential navigation tools for repository state
Professional README.md documents project vision and technical architecture
